extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, travel writers, and general writers seeking craft & productive habits
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice on writing novels and travel books, combining craft (plot, character, tone) with disciplined work habits, production metrics, and ethical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily task system / diary and quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: When I have commenced a new book, I have always prepared a diary, divided into weeks, and carried it on for the period which I have allowed myself for the completion of the work. In this I have entered, day by day, the number of pages I have written ... According to the circumstances ... I have allotted myself so many pages a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a dated weekly diary recording pages written each day; set a weekly pages quota based on circumstances; use the visible record of any shortfall to force compensatory work. The diary functions as a self-imposed law and taskmaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative production metrics (page and word counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a page is an ambiguous term, my page has been made to contain 250 words; and as words, if not watched, will have a tendency to straggle, I have had every word counted as I went.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a page (Trollope uses 250 words) and count words as you write. Set and track averages (he cites an average ~40 pages/week, range 20–112) and never deliver a contracted work short of the agreed size; aim for small excesses only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing work within proposed time and dimensions (timeliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have prided myself especially in completing it within the proposed time,--and I have always done so. There has ever been the record before me, and a week passed with an insufficient number of pages has been a blister to my eye ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor contractual timeframes and length requirements. Maintain a buffer so that 'needed pages' are kept ahead in the drawer to avoid anxiety and late delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of industry over waiting for inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: There are those who would be ashamed to subject themselves to such a taskmaster, and who think that the man who works with his imagination should allow himself to wait till--inspiration moves him. ... To me it would not be more absurd if the shoemaker were to wait for inspiration ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as a regular trade: sit at your desk daily and work regardless of whether you 'feel inspired'. Regular, disciplined work is the primary engine of output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small daily tasks beat spasmodic bursts (consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small daily task, if it be really daily, will beat the labours of a spasmodic Hercules. It is the tortoise which always catches the hare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor consistent daily progress over erratic, intense spurts; the cumulative effect of small, steady effort reliably outperforms irregular bursts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not scamp your work; maintain quality even with quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not on my conscience that I have ever scamped my work. My novels, whether good or bad, have been as good as I could make them. Had I taken three months of idleness between each they would have been no better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when producing many books, avoid rushing or cutting corners; regular productivity should not be an excuse for inferior workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is the vehicle; characters and portraiture matter more
rubrics_metrics.description: To my thinking, the plot is but the vehicle for all this; and when you have the vehicle without the passengers, a story of mystery in which the agents never spring to life, you have but a wooden show. There must, however, be a story. You must provide a vehicle of some sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a coherent story exists (the 'vehicle') but prioritize lively, believable characters who inhabit that plot; avoid plots that have little human vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: create portraits with known traits
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel should give a picture of common life enlivened by humour and sweetened by pathos. To make that picture worthy of attention, the canvas should be crowded with real portraits ... of created personages impregnated with traits of character which are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate your work with created characters who feel real by giving them recognizable traits and by portraying common life with humour and pathos. Characters should be composites, not mere copies of real people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone for novels: common life, humour, and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel should give a picture of common life enlivened by humour and sweetened by pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for balance: represent everyday life, use humour to enliven, and pathos to give emotional depth. This tonal mix will engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel-writing modes: facts versus vision (be explicit & honest)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of confidence which a reader may have in his author ... There is a confidence in facts and a confidence in vision. ... The former requires simple faith. The latter calls upon you to judge for yourself. ... Research is the weapon used by the former; observation by the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a travel piece aims to record verified facts (research-based) or to convey impressions (observation/currente calamo). Be honest to the reader about which mode you are using, since each carries different expectations about accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and acknowledgment; avoid plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: I think that an author, when he uses either the words or the plot of another, should own as much, demanding to be credited with no more of the work than he has himself produced. I may say also that I have never printed as my own a word that has been written by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When borrowing words or plots, acknowledge the source; do not present others' words or plots as wholly your own. Ethical transparency about sources is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose final-form prose directly when possible (for reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have taken infinite pains with these reports, habituating myself always to write them in the form in which they should be sent,--without a copy. It is by writing thus that a man can throw on to his paper the exact feeling with which his mind is impressed at the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For official or business prose, aim to write clean, final-form copy without drafts to capture immediacy and avoid wasted time in repeated redrafting; this presumes sufficient craft to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity over red-tape in official writing
rubrics_metrics.description: I had learned so to write my reports that they who read them should know what it was that I meant them to understand. But I do not think that they were regarded with favour. I have heard horror expressed because the old forms were disregarded and language used which had no savour of red-tape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear, readable prose in reports and official documents rather than obscure, formulaic language. Make your meaning plain to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain health and moderation to sustain work
rubrics_metrics.description: The author wants that as does every other workman,--that and a habit of industry. ... Mens sana in corpore sano. If the man whose business it is to write has eaten too many good things, or has drunk too much, or smoked too many cigars,--as men who write sometimes will do,--then his condition may be unfavourable for work ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain regular physical and mental health (moderation in eating, drinking, smoking) to keep consistent writing productivity; good habits support reliable output.
